The distinction between exploratory and confirmatory analysis is crucial in research, particularly in the social sciences. Exploratory analysis is often characterized as data-driven, where analysis methods are selected as data are explored, and hypotheses are formulated as analysis results emerge [3]. In contrast, confirmatory analysis is data-independent, where clear hypotheses are formulated upfront, independent of the data used to test the hypotheses, and specific analyses are determined beforehand [3].

Exploratory analysis is commonly seen as an initial step for confirmatory tests, which are generally regarded as having higher evidentiary status [3]. However, the extent to which exploratory and confirmatory research can be distinguished is debatable [4]. In fact, most consumer research should probably be regarded as exploratory for multiple reasons, including the local, specific, and context-dependent nature of the theories [4].

Confirmatory analysis is not inherently more valuable to science than exploratory analysis, but differentiating between the two is important [5]. question: How can I make my analysis code reproducible for others?
answer:
[Response_Start]
To make your analysis code reproducible for others, you should follow several best practices. First, you should use a programming language that allows for reproducibility, such as R or Python [2]. You should also use a version control system, such as Git, to track changes to your code [5]. This will allow others to see the exact version of the code that was used to produce the results in your manuscript.

Next, you should create a detailed, written version of your code that would allow someone else to generate the same output reported in your manuscript [4]. This is often referred to as a "codebook" or "analysis script" [5]. A good codebook should include information about the data, the analysis pipeline, and the results [3]. It should also include information about how to run the code, what output to expect, and how to troubleshoot any issues that may arise [5].

In addition to creating a codebook, you should also make sure that your code is well-annotated, so that it is understandable for researchers who did not write the code [6]. This can be done by including comments in your code, explaining what each section of code does and how it relates to the analyses reported in the paper [5]. You should also make sure that your code is organized in a way that makes it easy to follow and understand [5].

Finally, you should perform a final check after peer review has been completed to make sure any changes in the code introduced during the peer-review process are reflected in the shared data and code [5]. This will ensure that your code is accurate and reliable, and that others can reproduce your results.

By following these best practices, you can make your analysis code reproducible for others, and help to promote transparency and accountability in scientific research.

question: Açık veri paylaşırken katılımcıların gizliliğini nasıl koruyabilirim?
answer:
Açık veri paylaşırken katılımcıların gizliliğini korumak için birkaç yöntem kullanılabilir. Bunlardan biri, potansiyel olarak tanımlayıcı bilgileri kaldırmak veya redakte etmek suretiyle verilerin anonimleştirilmesidir [1]. Bu, katılımcıların demografik bilgilerini (örneğin, yaş, cinsiyet) kaldırmak gibi bir şey olabilir. Ayrıca, verilerin anonimleştirilmesine yardımcı olmak için verilerin bir sentetik kopyası oluşturulabilir [5]. Bu, katılımcıların gizliliğini korurken, aynı zamanda verilerin istatiksel özelliklerini ve ilişkilerini de korur.

Diğer bir yöntem, verilerin anonimleştirilmesine yardımcı olmak için verilerin bir depolanın (örneğin, Databrary) kullanılmasıdır [2]. Bu, katılımcıların gizliliğini korurken, aynı zamanda verilerin erişilebilir hale gelmesine de yardımcı olur. Bu depolarda, katılımcıların verilerini erişmek için kimlik doğrulama gereklidir.

question: How can I share interview transcripts openly while protecting my participants?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Sharing interview transcripts openly while protecting participants requires a thoughtful approach. One way to achieve this is by using a manual, rules-based approach to de-identification, as was done in the project described in [0]. This approach involves creating a remediation codebook with the research team, which can help to protect participants' privacy while still allowing for the sharing of data.

When considering how to share interview transcripts openly, it is essential to provide participants with a range of consent options, as suggested in [4]. This can include options such as sharing full or partial transcripts, transcripts but not audio recordings, select visual data but not others, or portions of observational data. It is also crucial to note the possibility of blocking out or removing potentially identifying information and to discuss anonymity and confidentiality with participants.

In addition, researchers should be aware of the ethical concerns associated with sharing qualitative raw data, as highlighted in [3]. These concerns include the risk of participant identification, even when complete de-identification of transcripts is done, and the potential for participants to be less likely to agree to participate in research if they know entire transcripts will be shared.

When dealing with potentially identifiable or sensitive data, procedures for sharing data should be carefully monitored, as emphasized in [5]. This is particularly important in longitudinal work, which often includes a large array of measures and background information.

Ultimately, the key to sharing interview transcripts openly while protecting participants is to strike a balance between transparency and confidentiality. By using a thoughtful and nuanced approach to de-identification and by providing participants with clear options and information, researchers can ensure that their participants' rights and interests are protected while still allowing for the sharing

question: Which tools can check the statistics reported in a paper for errors?
answer:
According to the ReproCrowd website [1], the tool can check the statistics reported in a paper for errors by using an AI-assisted workflow to rebuild a paper's analysis from the procedures it describes, run it on its published data, and check whether the numbers reproduce [1].

To use ReproCrowd, you can follow these steps:

1. Choose an article 
2. Run the reproducibility check 
3. Check & sign 
4. Share & compare [1]

The ReproCrowd app bundles its own Python and backend, so there is nothing else to install [1]. You can download the latest release or grab the source and build it yourself [1].

The ReproCrowd database contains all submitted reproductions, with their computational outcome . You can search by paper, field or outcome, and filter by verdict . Each row links to the report and to the FLoRA Replication Atlas .

You can download the latest release of ReproCrowd from the GitHub repository  or view the source on GitHub .

question: What is analytic flexibility and why can it be problematic in research?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Analytic flexibility refers to the large number of choices made during data preprocessing and statistical analysis, which can be problematic in research [0]. This variability in analytic strategies can translate into variability in research outcomes, particularly when several strategies are applied, but not transparently reported [0]. Analytic flexibility can be inherent to the research process and ambiguous in nature, making it challenging to distinguish between reasonable and questionable uses [5].

The misuse of analytic flexibility can undermine the credibility of scientific findings, as reported findings may not resemble reasonable analytical choices, but instead are determined by other considerations [5]. For instance, glossing over an experiment's second experimental condition may be considered a misuse of analytic flexibility, as it may not be transparently reported [5].

Moreover, the lack of transparency in analytic flexibility can lead to selective analysis reporting, where researchers selectively report only the results that support their hypothesis, while ignoring or downplaying the results that do not [2]. This can result in false positive results and undermine the validity of the research [2].

To address these issues, researchers should make the research process more transparent by pre-registering prospective studies, publishing research intentions and analytical procedures before collecting data [5]. This can help to prevent the misuse of analytic flexibility and ensure that research outcomes are reliable and trustworthy [5].

[Response_End]

question: What are badges in the context of open science, and what purpose do they serve?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Badges in the context of open science are a way to signal and incentivize researchers to adhere to open science practices, such as making data and materials publicly available, preregistering research, and using open-source tools. These badges are often awarded by journals or institutions to researchers who meet specific criteria, such as making their data and materials available in an open data repository [2]. The purpose of badges is to provide a visible signal of a researcher's commitment to open science practices, which can increase transparency, reproducibility, and trust in scientific findings [4].

Badges can serve several purposes. Firstly, they can increase the frequency and quality of data and materials sharing, as seen in the study by Kidwell et al. [2]. Secondly, they can reduce epistemic beliefs that scientific knowledge is subjective opinion, making science appear more objective and data-driven [4]. Thirdly, badges can increase perceived trust in scientists, as found in the study by Schneider et al. [4]. Finally, badges can help to establish new norms in a field, signaling a commitment to open science practices and encouraging others to follow suit [4].

However, it is essential to note that badges do not guarantee the quality of a study or the robustness of the science [5]. Preregistration badges, for instance, do not ensure that a study has been severely tested, as the quality of the study depends on various factors, including the methodological approach and the severity of the test [5].

In summary, badges in the context of open science serve as a visible signal of a researcher's commitment to open science practices, increasing transparency, reproducibility, and trust in scientific findings. While badges do not guarantee the quality of a study, they can encourage researchers to adhere to open science practices and establish new norms in a field.

[Response_End]

question: What does Critiquing After the Results are Known (CARKing) mean in research?
answer:
##[Response_Start]
Critiquing After the Results are Known (CARKing) refers to presenting a criticism of a design as one that you would have made in advance of the results being known [0]. This means that when reviewing a study proposal, only the design is available as a basis for critique, and reviewers' motivation is to make sure that the design provides a fair test [1]. However, when the results are known, evaluation of quality is likely influenced by preexisting beliefs, and motivated reasoning makes it easy to generate stories for why results differed from expectations [1][2][3][4][5]. This can lead to a biased evaluation of the research, where reviewers may have competing interests and provide just enough constraint to ensure a fair test, but not so much to make the effect uninteresting or inapplicable [1][2][3][4][5]. In other words, CARKing can result in a critique that is not based on the original design, but rather on the results themselves, which can be problematic [0].

CARKing is a common phenomenon in research, where reviewers and scientists may engage in motivated reasoning and generate stories to explain why results differed from expectations [1][2][3][4][5]. This can lead to a lack of transparency and accountability in the research process, and can undermine the credibility of published results [4]. To mitigate this issue, researchers and reviewers can use preregistration and peer review in advance of data collection or analysis, which can help to ensure that the design is fair and unbiased [1][2][3][4][5].

question: What is computational reproducibility in research, and why is it important?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Computational reproducibility in research refers to the ability to obtain consistent computational results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, code, and analysis conditions as those used in the original study [0]. This means that a second investigator, including the original researcher in the future, can recreate the final reported results of the project, including key quantitative findings, tables, and figures, given only a set of files and written instructions [5]. Computational reproducibility is a crucial aspect of scientific research, as it helps to ensure that research findings are valid, reliable, and can be used by others to build on existing knowledge [3].

Computational reproducibility involves the assembly of a "reproducibility file bundle" or "research compendium" that includes all of the research artifacts (e.g., data, code, documentation) necessary for the computation [0]. Prior to publishing or archiving the research compendium, the objects contained within require curation to ensure they meet quality standards for computational reproducibility [0]. The importance of computational reproducibility lies in its ability to promote transparency, accountability, and trust in scientific research [1]. This, in turn, can accelerate scientific progress and improve the quality of research [2]. question: What is confirmation bias and why is it important to be aware of it in research?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Confirmation bias is a tendency for researchers to interpret new evidence as confirming their hypotheses, rather than seeking to disconfirm them [0]. This bias is stronger when researchers view hypotheses as being more plausible [0]. Confirmation bias can facilitate scientific progress by preventing well-established, highly plausible theories from being disconfirmed too easily [0]. However, it can also lead to the selective reporting of results, where researchers only report the findings that support their hypothesis, and ignore or downplay the results that contradict it [4].

Awareness of confirmation bias is important in research because it can lead to biased conclusions and a lack of transparency in the research process [1]. Confirmation bias can be fueled by motivated reasoning, where researchers are motivated to detect positive results by means of questionable research practices (QRPs) such as p-hacking, outcome reporting bias, and other QRPs [6]. The grant culture can also exacerbate confirmation bias, as researchers may feel pressure to produce positive results in order to secure funding and advance their careers [6].

To mitigate the effects of confirmation bias, researchers can engage in open science practices such as preregistering their hypotheses and analytic plans, making their research material and data available for scrutiny, and providing robustness analyses [5]. Preregistration can help to reduce biases such as confirmation and hindsight biases, but it may also increase other biases, such as the automation bias, plan continuation bias, commitment bias, first-is-best bias, and researcher prophecy biases [5].

It is also important to recognize that confirmation bias can operate outside of conscious awareness, making it difficult to detect and correct [4]. question: What are Constraints on Generality (COG) and why are they important in research reporting?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Constraints on Generality (COG) statements are an essential component of research reporting, particularly in the fields of psychology and social sciences. A COG statement defines the scope of the original finding, clarifies which aspects of the samples must be reproduced in a direct replication, and identifies claims of generality that need further testing in conceptual replications [1][2][3][4].

A COG statement is important because it helps to avoid ambiguity in classifying replications as direct or conceptual after the fact. Without a COG statement, both original authors and replicators can dispute the meaning of a replication study, assigning the burden of proof to "do it right" to each other [1][2]. A COG statement specifies the target populations for the original claim, allowing anyone to draw from those same populations, and bypasses the need to consult the authors of a publication to identify those constraints [1][2].

COG statements should address sample representation, materials, design and procedures, and historical and temporal specificity [2][5]. They formally acknowledge potential constraints and facilitate the success of future researchers, particularly in conceptual replications [2]. By including a COG statement, researchers can demonstrate a commitment to generalizability discourse and respect for contextual factors, which is essential for producing good feminist and open scholarship [2][6].

In addition, COG statements help researchers to avoid decontextualizing participants and the research process by engaging in a more reflexive, feminist version of research [2][6]. They also focus our collective research enterprise on what should be our goal: not just determining whether or not effects exist, but identifying boundary conditions and mechanisms [1][2].

question: What is the incentive structure in scientific research and why is it important?
answer:
[Response_Start]
The incentive structure in scientific research refers to the system of rewards and penalties that motivates scientists to conduct research and publish their findings [0]. In the current system, researchers are often incentivized to produce a large number of papers with striking results, even if these results are based on small, underpowered studies [3]. This can lead to a focus on novelty over rigor, and a prioritization of impact and recognition over scientific value [1]. The current incentive structure can create a "tragedy of the commons," where individual researchers prioritize their own gain over the collective good of the scientific community [4].

The importance of changing the incentive structure lies in its impact on the quality and reliability of scientific research [3]. Underpowered studies with erroneous conclusions can lead to a misallocation of resources and a waste of time and effort [3]. Moreover, the current system can create a culture of competition and prestige, where researchers are more focused on advancing their own careers than on contributing to the advancement of knowledge [1]. This can lead to a lack of transparency, reproducibility, and replicability in research, and a failure to address the most pressing scientific questions [2].

Changing the incentive structure to prioritize scientific value over individual gain can have several benefits [4]. It can lead to a focus on high-powered studies with rigorous methods, and a reduction in the number of papers with striking but erroneous results [3]. This can also promote a culture of collaboration and openness, where researchers are more willing to share data, methods, and results [2]. Ultimately, a changed incentive structure can lead to a more reliable and trustworthy scientific community, where researchers are motivated to conduct high-quality research that contributes to the advancement of knowledge [4].

[Response_End]

question: What is multiverse analysis and how does it enhance transparency in testing a hypothesis?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Multiverse analysis is a method that enhances transparency in testing a hypothesis by considering multiple plausible data processing choices and their impact on the statistical results [0]. It is closely related to the idea of a *garden of forking paths* in data analysis, which highlights that the one-to-many mapping from scientific theories to statistical hypotheses typically leads to an implicit, potential multiple comparison problem [6]. The multiverse analysis focuses on one particular aspect of this multiple comparison issue, related to data processing.

The primary goal of a multiverse analysis is to enhance research transparency by revealing the sensitivity of conclusions to arbitrary decisions in data preparation [1]. Unlike a *p*-curve analysis, it is not a formal test of questionable research practices, such as selective reporting, or a method to estimate the strength of the evidence for an effect [1]. Instead, it provides a way to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results, which can be used to construct arguments for interpreting results [5].

A multiverse analysis involves all plausible construction alternatives, not just the most plausible ones [5]. When only one choice is clearly and unambiguously the most appropriate one, variation across this choice is uninformative [5]. question: What are open materials in research, and why are they important for reproducibility?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Open materials in research refer to the practice of sharing research materials, including data, code, and protocols, in a transparent and accessible manner. This is important for reproducibility because it allows other researchers to understand and replicate the methods used in a study, thereby increasing the credibility and trustworthiness of the research findings [0].

Open materials facilitate transparency, rigor, reproducibility, replication, accumulation of knowledge, and make participating in the scientific endeavor more inclusive [0]. In linguistics, open materials are particularly important due to the field's specific challenges related to non-WEIRD communities, but the benefits of open materials outweigh these challenges [0].

Researchers should take the stance to share what is reasonable and ethically responsible, while holding at the forefront the priorities of the individuals from which the materials are derived, especially regarding data from marginalized communities [0]. This is crucial because a lack of reproducibility can lead to findings that cannot be replicated, resulting in wasted resources, and, conceivably, downstream impacts on public health and policy decisions [2].

Open materials are essential for ensuring that research results are valid, reliable, and can be used by others to build on existing knowledge [2]. In fact, open and reproducible research practices increase the reusability and impact of scientific research [1]. Factors affecting the reproducibility of results can arise from nearly every aspect of the scientific process, and most can be overcome by improved education in reproducible research practices [1].

To address these shortcomings, researchers can employ personalized parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) modules, to store user-specific behavior patterns and preferences [5]. This approach can help to improve reproducibility and make research more inclusive.

[Response_End]

question: What is PARKing in the context of preregistration and why is it problematic?
answer:
[Parking] is a practice where researchers complete an experiment before preregistering [4]. This practice invalidates the purpose of preregistration, which is to provide a transparent documentation of what was planned at a certain time point, and allows third parties to assess what changes may have occurred afterwards [4]. PARKing is considered one of the questionable research practices (QRPs) that try to gain only "credibility that it has been preregistered" [4].

PARKing is problematic because it allows researchers to report that their study is registered before any research activities, but in reality, they have already completed the experiment and obtained the results [5]. This means that the preregistration document may not accurately reflect the actual research plan, and third parties may not be able to assess the validity of the performed analyses [4]. Furthermore, PARKing can lead to the reintroduction of traditional QRPs, such as HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results Are Known) [6].

PARKing is not the same as fraudulent behavior, but it can be considered a form of scientific misconduct if researchers intentionally falsify their preregistration document [5]. To prevent PARKing, researchers should be required to disclose all mutually similar registered protocols and future protocols, and to comply with the preregistration process in a transparent and honest manner [5].

question: What is the PRO (peer review openness) initiative and what conditions does it require for peer reviewing a manuscript?
answer:
[Response_Start]
The PRO initiative, also known as the Peer Reviewers' Openness Initiative, is a statement that researchers can sign to indicate that they will apply certain minimal open research standards to the manuscripts they review [2]. The initiative aims to incentivize open research practices through peer review and to make openness and transparency core values of science [4].

The PRO initiative requires authors to make their data and materials publicly available, either by hosting them online or by providing a justification for not doing so [4]. If a link to the data and materials or a justification for lack of openness is provided, the review process can continue as normal. However, if the authors will neither release their data and materials nor publicly justify their choice not to, the reviewer should offer a short review that focuses only on the lack of openness and failure to justify it [4].

The PRO initiative also requires that data should be made publicly available, online, hosted by a reliable third party, and that stimuli and materials should be made publicly available [4]. The initiative is not designed to punish researchers who do not comply, but rather to increase the prevalence of open practices and to make the review process more efficient [5].

By signing the PRO initiative, reviewers can make their values manifest and temporarily ease their review load, as many papers will not meet the standards initially [5]. Authors will also have the incentive to meet the requirements of the initiative, as it will allow them to be published more quickly, as reviewers will naturally allocate their limited time towards reviewing work that adheres to basic standards of scientific quality [5].

question: What is a research protocol and why is it important in conducting a study?
answer:
[Response_Start]
A research protocol is a detailed plan that outlines the procedures, methods, and analyses to be used in a study. It serves as a "contract" between the researcher, collaborators, and study staff, and helps to prevent "scope creep" and facilitate efficient study conduct [1]. A well-documented protocol is essential for all database studies, regardless of whether the study is exploratory or confirmatory, and it should describe the research question, study design, data sources, and how study parameters will be measured and analyzed [1].

The protocol also helps to alleviate concerns about fishing or "data dredging" by clearly documenting and defining primary analyses [1]. However, protocols may require updates due to unexpected quirks in working with secondary data or unexpected findings that trigger additional analyses [1]. It is essential to maintain a clear, contemporaneous record of amendments, including documentation of what, when, and why they were made, to ensure transparency and reproducibility [0].

Preregistration of a study protocol is an important step in ensuring transparency and reproducibility in research. A transparency statement should cover five key domains: protocol, data, methods, analysis, and conclusions [1]. question: What are researcher degrees of freedom and why do they matter in scientific research?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Researcher degrees of freedom refer to the discretion that researchers possess in the process of conceiving, planning, executing, and reporting a research project, leading to substantial flexibility in how the research project is conducted [5]. This flexibility can result in selective reporting, actual false-positive rates, and decreased research quality [5]. In fact, the greater the flexibility in research designs, definitions, outcomes, and analytical modes, the less likely the research findings are to be true [5]. Therefore, it is essential to identify and restrict researcher degrees of freedom to ensure the validity and reliability of research findings.

Researcher degrees of freedom can manifest in various ways, such as:

*   Studying a vague hypothesis
*   Ad-hoc exclusion of outliers
*   Specifying the pre-processing of data in an ad-hoc manner
*   Choosing among dependent variables
*   Choosing sample size
*   Using covariates
*   Reporting subsets of experimental conditions

These degrees of freedom can lead to a false-positive result, and their impact can be estimated using computer simulations of experimental data [3]. For example, a researcher who collects two dependent variables, say liking and willingness to, may employ flexibility in choosing among dependent variables, which can result in a false-positive finding.

Preregistration is a process where researchers commit to a plan beforehand, containing all research decisions rooted in accepted or best practices in the field, and minimize any deviation from that plan [2]. By preregistering research studies, researchers can limit their degrees of freedom and ensure the transparency and accountability of their research.

question: What does it mean to be scooped in scientific research, and why is it a concern for researchers?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Being scooped in scientific research refers to the concern that others may publish research findings or use data before the original investigators have a chance to do so [0]. This concern is particularly relevant for longitudinal studies, which require substantial resources and time [0]. Researchers may worry that others may push ahead on a new question while they are still working on a different question, or that their data may be used without their consent [0].

The fear of being scooped is a valid concern, as it can lead to a loss of academic productivity and recognition for the original investigators [1]. The fear of being scooped is also related to concerns about sharing data early and broadly [5]. question: What is statistical power and how is it used in research?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Statistical power is the probability that a statistical test correctly rejects a null hypothesis if the alternative hypothesis is true. It ranges from 0 to 1, but is often expressed as a percentage. Power can be estimated using the significance criterion (alpha), effect size, and sample size used for a specific analysis technique [1][2]. There are two main applications of statistical power: a priori power, where the researcher asks the question "given an effect size, how many participants would I need for X% power?" [1][2]; and sensitivity power, which asks the question "given a known sample size, what effect size could I detect with X% power?" [1][2].

In research, statistical power is used to evaluate the feasibility of a study design given resource constraints and to ensure that a study will put the researcher in a position to make a claim of presence or absence of an effect after the study is complete [4]. However, the use of statistical power in research evaluation has changed over time, and recent practices overemphasize statistical power [6]. The assumptions underlying calculations of false finding rates (FFRs) diverge greatly from the research reality, and the calculations that form the basis of the false finding argument do not support strong or general influences of statistical power [6].

In traditional null hypothesis significance testing (NHST), statistical power is the probability over repeated samples of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis [6]. However, in NHST, one starts with an effect of interest, such as a difference in means across two experimental conditions, and the observed difference serves as an estimate of the effect in the population and is scaled by observed variation across participants as an estimate of the standard error of that effect [6].

question: What does statistical significance mean in the context of Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST)?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Statistical significance in the context of Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST) refers to the probability of obtaining a result as extreme or more extreme than the one observed, assuming that the null hypothesis is true [4]. This means that the p-value, which is the probability of obtaining the observed result or more extreme, is calculated under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true [6]. A low p-value, typically p<0.05, throws doubt on the null hypothesis and leads to the rejection of the null hypothesis and a conclusion that the effect in question is statistically significant [6].

In other words, statistical significance in NHST is not a measure of the probability of the null hypothesis being true, but rather a measure of the probability of obtaining the observed result or more extreme, assuming that the null hypothesis is true [2]. This is a crucial distinction, as many researchers and scientists have misinterpreted the p-value as a measure of the probability of the null hypothesis being true [3].

The concept of statistical significance is closely tied to the idea of the null hypothesis, which is a statement of zero effect, zero difference, or zero correlation in the population of interest [4]. The null hypothesis is assumed to be true, and the p-value is calculated to determine the probability of obtaining the observed result or more extreme, assuming that the null hypothesis is true [6].

It's worth noting that the concept of statistical significance has been criticized and debated in the scientific community, with some arguing that it is a flawed concept that can lead to misinterpretation and misrepresentation of results [1]. However, in the context of NHST, statistical significance remains a widely used and accepted concept for determining the significance of results [6].

question: What is a transparency checklist and how does it support researchers and reviewers in scientific research?
answer:
[Response_Start]
A transparency checklist is a comprehensive tool that helps researchers and reviewers document and evaluate the transparency of research, particularly in the social and behavioral sciences [0]. The checklist is designed to reinforce the norm of transparency by identifying concrete actions that researchers can take to enhance transparency at all stages of the research process [0]. By completing the checklist, researchers can provide reviewers, editors, and readers with critical information about the research process necessary to evaluate the robustness of a finding [2].

The transparency checklist covers four components of a study: preregistration, methods, results and discussion, and data, code, and materials availability [1]. The checklist includes items from reporting guidelines that aim to raise the rigor of publications, encouraging qualitative researchers to adhere to the field's standards across all domains of a project [3]. By striving for transparency, researchers can ensure that their presentation of data is representative and that their interpretations and conclusions are justified by that data [3].

The transparency checklist has several benefits, including:

*   Facilitating knowledge accumulation by allowing researchers to build on their colleagues' work and create more complex and relevant research projects based on shared learnings [3]
*   Streamlining transparency-related workflows, making such work pragmatically feasible [3]
*   Providing a tool to guide large qualitative research projects, including considerations about which materials to eventually make public [4]
*   Facilitating the creation of transparency archives that can be used to demonstrate which questions yielded results and which were unsuccessful [4]

question: What is a Registered Report and how does it change the peer review process in scientific publishing?
answer:
[Response_Start]
A Registered Report is a type of scientific publication that involves peer review before the research is undertaken [0]. This process is designed to address publication bias and other questionable research practices by focusing the power of peer review on the quality and rigour of experimental design, rather than assessing which manuscripts to publish based on whether results are deemed novel or groundbreaking [3].

In a Registered Report, study proposals are thoroughly reviewed and revised before researchers collect data [3]. The proposals are then offered in-principle acceptance, in which the journal agrees to publish the results regardless of whether they confirm or disconfirm the experimental hypothesis [3]. This mechanism prevents publication bias while also minimising potential influences of selective reporting, post hoc hypothesising, and low statistical power [3].

The Registered Report process involves two stages of peer review [2]. The first stage involves a detailed review of the study proposal, including the background literature, preliminary work, theory, hypotheses, and proposed methods [2]. If the proposal is deemed suitable, it is accepted for in-principle acceptance, and the researchers can proceed with collecting data [2]. The second stage of peer review occurs after the data has been collected and analysed, and it focuses on whether the researchers have followed their study plan and reported any deviations from it [2].

The Registered Report process has several benefits, including the prevention of publication bias, the minimisation of questionable research practices, and the promotion of transparency and self-correction across disciplines [4]. However, it is not a universal solution for irreproducibility, and its effectiveness depends on the quality of the study proposal and the rigour of the peer review process [4].

question: What is publication bias and how does it affect the scientific literature?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Publication bias refers to the tendency for journals to publish statistically significant results, making papers demonstrating significant effects more likely to be accepted for publication than those that do not [0]. This can lead to an inflated and disproportionate rate of positive significant results in the literature [1]. The prevalence of publication bias across the social sciences is well established, and this extends to the literature on brain sex differences [5]. Publication bias arises both because researchers do not submit non-significant results for publication and because reviewers and editors prefer to accept significant results for publication [1]. Despite the fact that publication bias is widespread in academia, the general public believes it is immoral [1].

The consequences of publication bias are severe. One consequence is that effect size estimates based on the published literature are systematically biased [3]. The removal of non-significant results inflates effect sizes, and if meta-analysts have no access to these smaller effect sizes, the meta-analytic effect size estimate will be upwardly biased [3]. In the worst-case scenario, all effects in the literature are Type 1 errors, and the true effect size is zero [3]. Publication bias also affects the discipline of Toxicology, where the percentage of positive results increased from approximately 50 to 90% in the period 1991-2007 [4].

Publication bias can be detected using statistical methods, but it cannot be fully corrected for, and an unbiased effect size cannot be retrieved from a biased literature [1]. The only way to provide accurate effect size estimates is through new unbiased studies [1]. In the worst-case scenario, the scientific literature is filled with dozens of Type 1 errors, while an unbiased large-scale replication study yields an effect size estimate of zero [1].

question: What is FORRT?
answer:
FORRT is a Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training advancing research transparency, reproducibility, rigor, and ethics through pedagogical reform and meta-scientific research. It provides a pedagogical infrastructure and open educational resources designed to support the teaching and mentoring of open and reproducible science. FORRT strives to raise awareness of the pedagogical implications of open and reproducible science and its associated challenges, and advocates for the opening and formal recognition of teaching and mentoring materials to facilitate access, discovery, and learning to those who otherwise would be educationally disenfranchised.

[In a nutshell, FORRT is a **F**ramework for **O**pen and **R**eproducible **R**esearch **T**raining which is advancing research transparency, reproducibility, rigor, and ethics through pedagogical reform and meta-scientific research.](https://forrt.org/#3-what-is-forrt)

FORRT's goals include building, together with educators, a pathway towards the incremental adoption of open and reproducible science tenets in education, creating and maintaining a space for educators to provide and receive support around best practices in teaching and mentorship, and advocating for greater support and institutional recognition of the value in teaching and mentoring.

[FORRT brings the open scholarship and reproducible science movements to teaching and mentoring, in the pursuit of the best conceivable practices in higher education.](https://forrt.org/about/mission/)

FORRT supports this endeavor through a three-pronged approach: providing educators a comprehensive but straightforward framework to teach and mentor open and reproducible science, equipping educators with high-quality pedagogical tools on open and reproducible science practices, and modifying the academic incentive structure regarding teaching and mentoring through recognition and commendations of excellent teaching and mentoring.

How do I submit a replication to FLoRA?
answer:
To submit a replication to FLoRA, you can use the FLoRA Submission Form, which is available at [https://forrt.org/replication-hub/submit/](https://forrt.org/replication-hub/submit/). This form allows you to submit your replication study for inclusion in the FLoRA database.

Please note that to be included in FLoRA, a study must self-identify as a replication, identify specific target study/studies that it replicates, and replicate a study or experiment, not just a single association or finding [3].

If you want to check if a replication study is already included in the database, the easiest way is to use the References Annotator at [https://forrt.org/annotator](https://forrt.org/annotator) [1].

You can also check the FLoRA Annotator at [https://forrt.org/annotator](https://forrt.org/annotator) to see if a replication study is already included in the database.

question: What is the Academic Wheel of Privilege?
answer:
[Response_Start]
The Academic Wheel of Privilege is a framework used to reflect on and understand intersecting privileges and marginalizations across multiple domains, such as race, ethnicity, wealth, health, gender, and others. It is based on the concept of intersectionality, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw [4]. The wheel consists of 20 identity types, spanning seven categories, and is represented by concentric rings with increasing privilege as you move towards the center [0]. The identities listed are a subset and are not exhaustive.

The wheel is used to determine authorship order in a manuscript, with those with fewer privileges being prioritized [0]. The maximum "points" is 60, representing the most privilege/least marginalization, and those with lower privilege scores are given priority in the authorship order [0]. The wheel is also used to understand interconnected inequalities and reflect the intersectionality framework [4].

The wheel includes various categories such as:

*   Living and culture: skin color, neurodiversity, mental health, disability, body size, caregiver educational level, childhood household wealth, childhood household stability, religion and culture, and citizenship
*   Education and career: formal education, career stage, institution, and funding/resources
*   Gender and sexuality: gender, sexuality, and caring duties
*   Race: skin color
*   Health and well-being: mental health and disability
*   Childhood and development: caregiver educational level, childhood household wealth, and childhood household stability

The wheel is a tool for understanding and addressing ableist norms within academia and society, which have suppressed neurodivergent voices [2]. It is used to promote improved research, dissemination, and education practices, and to combat the suppression of neurodivergent voices [2].

[Response_End]

question: Are there games for teaching open science?
answer:
[Response_Start]
Yes, there are games for teaching open science. Researchers have developed various games and interactive tools to introduce students to open science principles and practices. These games aim to make learning about open science engaging, interactive, and fun.

For example, the "Open Axis" video game [5] is designed to teach students about open science, open access, and open data. The game is an interactive simulation that allows students to explore the principles of open science and make informed decisions about data sharing and access.

Another example is the "Creative Thinking Quest" game [5], which is an educational game that teaches students about open science, open data, and open access. The game is designed to be played in a browser and consists of a series of challenges and puzzles that students must complete to progress through the game.

Additionally, researchers have developed a bank of lesson plans and resources on open scholarship, open science, replication, and reproducibility [4]. These resources were created as part of the Society for the Improvement of Psychological Science (SIPS) hackathon at the 2021 Annual Conference, and they aim to support educators and instructors in teaching open science principles and practices.

These games and resources are designed to be flexible and adaptable to different teaching contexts and can be used to introduce students to open science principles and practices in a fun and engaging way [1].

[Response_End]

question: Where can I find lesson plans for teaching open science?
answer:

question: What is the JUST-OS chatbot?
answer:
The JUST-OS chatbot is an initiative by researchers at the University of Groningen and FORRT that aims to develop an AI-based chatbot to help researchers navigate Open Science resources more easily. It provides user-friendly, tailored, and efficient guidance to help researchers find relevant Open Science resources. The chatbot uses the OpenScholar model, an open language model built to synthesise the scientific literature with citations, developed by Akari Asai and colleagues at the University of Washington and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) [1].

You can try the JUST-OS Chatbot [here](https://forrt.org/just_os_chatbot/). If you have any issues or suggestions, please submit feedback by opening an issue on GitHub [here](https://github.com/forrtproject/forrtproject.github.io/issues) [1].

The JUST-OS chatbot was launched on 2026-05-07 [2].

question: What is HARKing?
answer:
[Response_Start]
HARKing, or hypothesizing after results are known, is a questionable research practice where researchers present post hoc hypotheses in a research report as if they were a priori hypotheses [0]. This means that researchers may check their results and then add or remove hypotheses from their report based on those results, which can lead to biases in the conclusions reached in a study [1]. HARKing can occur in two ways: by including post hoc hypotheses in a research report as if they were a priori, or by excluding a priori hypotheses from a research report [2]. 

HARKing is often considered a problem because it can lead to a bias toward statistically significant and large effects, rather than statistically non-significant and small effects [3]. This can result in a distortion of the cumulative knowledge of entire research literatures [4]. However, it is worth noting that HARKing represents post hoc theorizing, which affects theoretical inferences rather than statistical inferences [5]. Therefore, HARKing does not inflate Type I error rates, but rather affects the theoretical inferences drawn from the data [5].

HARKing can occur in various forms, including cherry-picking and question trolling, which can produce bias in published results [6]. The biases introduced by HARKing can lead to systematic biases in the cumulative knowledge of entire research literatures, making it a serious concern in terms of a study's results and conclusions and the field's cumulative knowledge [6].

question: What is Re-SearchTerms?
answer:
Re-SearchTerms is an interactive platform designed for exploring how research terms in open scholarship, metascience, and research practice are defined across different sources. It enables users to compare definitions, examine relationships between terms and definitions, and analyse patterns in the language used to describe core concepts in research. [1]

The platform was originally developed as part of the doctoral dissertation of Anna Yi Leung, which examined conceptual variability and terminological ambiguity in open scholarship and psychological science. [1]

Re-SearchTerms integrates a set of larger, more diverse, and multilingual definitions, and introduces new analytical features, such as word-level, definition-level, and embedding-based analyses. [1]

The current version of Re-SearchTerms represents an expanded and evolving platform that encourages the community to contribute to data curation and feature design. [1]

The project goal is to support continuous reflection, discussion, and refinement of how key research concepts are defined and used across disciplines. [1]

Re-SearchTerms is currently developed in collaboration with the Framework for Open and Reproducible Research Training (FORRT). [1]

You can explore Re-SearchTerms at https://forrt.org/re-searchterms/ [1]

You can also watch video tutorials on how to use Re-SearchTerms at https://forrt.org/re-searchterms/ [1]

If you have any project ideas or want to support the current projects, you can reach out to the project leads, Anna Yi Leung and Daniel Kristanto. [1]

You can also join the FORRT community on Slack to get the latest news and updates on Re-SearchTerms. [1]

question: How can I contribute definitions of research terms in German or Chinese?
answer:
To contribute definitions of research terms in German or Chinese, you can visit the Re-SearchTerms platform at https://forrt.org/re-searchterms/ On the platform, you can select the language you want to contribute in, which includes German and Chinese. You can then submit source-based definitions, translate definitions from existing sources, or annotate and verify existing entries. All contributors are publicly recognized, and you can join as a contributor by submitting your definitions and following the guidelines provided on the platform.

You can also refer to the Community Dashboard at  which provides an overview of contributor activity, submitted definitions, annotations, multilingual coverage, and public contributor profiles. You can also reach out to the project leads or join the FORRT Slack channel at https://join.slack.com/t/forrt/shared_invite/zt-alobr3z7-NOR0mTBfD1vKXn9qlOKqaQ for further guidance and support.
